Lead Abatement in Detroit, MI

Most of Detroit's housing predates the 1978 ban on lead paint, which makes old coatings a fair assumption until a test says otherwise. Whether you found peeling paint on a porch, received a rental notice or plan to remodel, start by describing what you see and we will point you to the right lead service.

What toxic lead abatement actually covers

Most people searching for lead abatement are really trying to answer a smaller question first: does my house have a lead problem, and what kind? The word covers a chain of separate services. A lead paint inspection finds lead paint. A risk assessment finds hazards. Abatement itself, meaning lead paint removal, replacement, enclosure or encapsulation, is the permanent fix, and clearance testing confirms the dust is gone afterward.

Detroit adds a local layer. The city's Buildings, Safety Engineering and Environmental Department now describes a 15-point property-condition inspection for rental certificates, while older city guidance still lists a separate lead-report step. Rental owners should confirm the current requirement with BSEED rather than rely on an old checklist.

Michigan also controls who may do this work. The state runs an authorized lead-based paint activities program, and Michigan's hiring guidance distinguishes inspectors, risk assessors and abatement firms, so one of the first questions to ask anyone is which credential fits your job.

How do I know if I need lead abatement or just testing?

Does my Detroit house have lead paint?

If it was built before 1978, it might. Much of Detroit's housing predates the 1978 ban, and the older the house, the more likely lead paint is. Testing is the only way to know which surfaces carry it.

Is lead abatement different from a renovation?

Yes. Abatement is done to permanently eliminate lead hazards. Renovation disturbs paint as a side effect and needs lead-safe work practices.

Who can test for lead in Michigan?

Lead Paint Testing and Inspection for Detroit Homes

Is that peeling paint actually lead? Color, texture and the age of a house cannot answer that question. A lead-based paint inspection identifies lead paint and its location. It is the right starting point when your main question is what materials you are about to disturb.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

What testing can tell you

An inspector may use an XRF instrument or laboratory analysis of paint samples. Ask which surfaces will be tested and whether the written report identifies components by room. A quick consumer swab is not a substitute for a documented professional inspection when a regulated report is needed.

Inspection or risk assessment?

An inspection locates lead paint. A risk assessment looks for current hazards and recommends controls. EPA explains why these are different services. If paint chips, window dust or bare soil are the concern, describe those conditions rather than requesting a paint test alone.

Prepare for the visit

Gather the construction date, any previous lead reports and a list of planned work. Mention doors, stair rails, porch surfaces and original window sashes. Testing should happen before sanding, scraping or demolition changes the condition of those surfaces.

Common questions

Who can perform a lead paint inspection in Michigan?

Michigan runs an authorized lead-based paint activities program that certifies inspectors, risk assessors and abatement firms. Ask for the credential that matches the task before you schedule.

Is a general home inspection the same as a lead inspection?

No. A general home inspection does not identify lead paint surface by surface. A lead-based paint inspection uses XRF or laboratory analysis and produces a room-by-room record.

Do I need testing before a small remodel?

If the house predates 1978 and the work disturbs paint, identify the coatings first. Testing should happen before sanding, scraping or demolition changes the condition of those surfaces.

Lead Risk Assessment for Detroit Homes and Rentals

Dust keeps returning to the window sill. Paint is flaking near a toddler’s play area. A risk assessment starts with the condition of the home and the ways someone could encounter lead, then turns findings into a plan.

A report that connects the dots

A certified risk assessor evaluates deteriorated paint and may collect dust or soil samples. The report should describe hazards, their locations and options for dealing with them. Tell the assessor about recent renovations, accessible exterior soil and rooms used by children.

Choose the right professional

Michigan explains how to hire a lead professional and distinguishes inspectors, risk assessors and abatement firms. Verify current certifications for the particular task. An EPA renovation certificate is not interchangeable with Michigan abatement or risk-assessment qualifications.

A health result is not a building diagnosis

If a child has an elevated blood lead result, follow the healthcare provider’s advice and contact the local health department. A home assessment can investigate environmental sources, but this website cannot diagnose exposure or determine medical treatment. Do not assume paint is the only possible source.

Who can perform a lead risk assessment in Michigan?

Michigan distinguishes inspectors, risk assessors and abatement firms, and each task has its own credential. Verify the current certification for the specific work before you hire.

What does the report give me?

The report describes the hazards found, their locations and the options for controlling them, so the work that follows targets documented conditions rather than guesses.

A child's test came back high. Is this the right step?

Follow the healthcare provider's advice and contact the local health department first. A home assessment can investigate environmental sources, but it cannot diagnose exposure or replace medical guidance.

Lead Dust and Soil Hazard Control for Detroit Homes

The room may look clean while fine lead dust remains on floors and window troughs. Outside, deteriorating coatings can contaminate nearby soil. Professional sampling helps separate a visible mess from a measured hazard.

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Dust is not ordinary household dirt

Describe when dust appeared, whether work disturbed painted surfaces and which rooms or entry routes are affected. A professional plan may include specialized HEPA cleaning and wet-cleaning methods. Do not use a household vacuum as a substitute for a lead cleanup plan.

A bare patch outside can need assessment

Ask a risk assessor whether soil sampling is warranted around the drip line, a play area or other accessible ground. Paint chips in the soil do not establish the laboratory concentration. The control method depends on findings and site conditions, not a photograph of the yard.

Verify the outcome

EPA distinguishes paint, dust and soil hazards in risk assessments. When clearance is required, appearance alone does not establish a pass. Ask who samples, which laboratory analyzes the samples and what documentation you will receive.

Common questions

Can I just vacuum up the dust?

A household vacuum is not a substitute for a lead cleanup plan. Professional plans use specialized HEPA and wet-cleaning methods.

How do I know if my yard soil has lead?

Only sampling establishes the concentration. Ask a risk assessor whether soil sampling is warranted around the drip line, play areas or other accessible ground.

When is clearance required?

It depends on the project and the requirement behind the work. Ask who samples, which laboratory analyzes the samples and what documentation you will receive.

Lead Paint Removal and Abatement in Detroit, MI

Removing lead paint is not a normal repainting job. The work can create contaminated dust if it is done without the right controls. Start with the inspection or risk-assessment report so the abatement scope targets documented hazards.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Removal is one option, not the only option

EPA describes abatement as permanent hazard elimination. Depending on the surface and its condition, a plan may use component replacement, enclosure, approved encapsulation or removal. Compare these choices with a qualified professional rather than assuming every painted surface must be stripped.

What belongs in the scope

Ask for the surfaces and rooms included, the containment plan, how occupants will be protected, cleanup procedures and the clearance arrangements. Discuss whether people or pets must leave the work area and who handles contaminated waste. Do not accept a verbal promise that ordinary painting will permanently solve a documented hazard.

Before work starts

Verify Michigan firm and individual credentials. Review any building permits or historic-district approvals separately. Avoid dry sanding or scraping suspect paint yourself while waiting. A price depends on the findings, access and chosen method, not a flat cost per house.

Common questions

Does every lead-painted surface have to be stripped?

No. Depending on the surface and its condition, a plan may use component replacement, enclosure, approved encapsulation or removal. Compare the options before assuming everything comes off.

Can I scrape the paint myself while I wait?

EPA advises against removing lead-based paint yourself. Avoid dry sanding or scraping suspect paint, and use trained, certified people for work that disturbs it.

What should a written abatement scope include?

The surfaces and rooms included, the containment plan, occupant protection, cleanup procedures and the clearance arrangements, plus who handles contaminated waste.

Corktown: planning a lead-safe renovation before the first scrape

Corktown’s older homes are part of what makes the neighborhood recognizable. When a project involves porch trim, windows or painted interiors, keeping that character should start with knowing what materials the work will disturb.

Why the local context matters

The Detroit Historical Society documents Corktown’s Federal-style houses and later Victorian buildings, along with the neighborhood’s historic-district status. That history supports checking building records and painted components early. It does not prove that any particular house contains lead. A test, not a neighborhood name, answers that question.

Write the project before choosing the method

List each component you plan to change: sash, frame, porch rail, exterior trim or room finish. Keep the inspection report with that list. If the concern is dust from a rubbing window, ask whether a risk assessment and component-specific control are more useful than a whole-house stripping proposal. Different surfaces may need different solutions.

Preservation approval is a separate step

For a property inside a local historic district, discuss exterior work with Detroit’s Historic District Commission before ordering or removing components. A lead professional can develop a hazard-control plan, but that plan does not grant preservation approval. Bring both sets of requirements into the written scope so they do not conflict halfway through the job.

Do not create the hazard while investigating it

Avoid sanding suspect paint to “see what is underneath.” EPA’s renovation guidance explains why paid disturbance of paint in applicable older housing requires lead-safe practices. Ask the firm about qualifications, containment, occupant protection and cleanup. If the purpose is permanent hazard elimination, verify abatement qualifications rather than relying on an RRP certificate alone.

A useful first request

Send the building age if known, the project list, any earlier lead report and photos of deteriorated surfaces. Photos describe a condition; they are not a lead test. Ask what evaluation is needed before work and what final documentation will show the project is complete. No neighborhood-wide promise can replace a property-specific scope.

Common questions

Do I need Historic District Commission approval for a Corktown renovation?

For a property inside the local historic district, discuss exterior work with the Commission before ordering or removing components. A lead plan does not grant preservation approval.

Can I test the paint before the renovation plan is final?

Yes, and that is the right order. Bring the project list to the inspection so the report identifies the components the work will disturb.

Boston-Edison: original windows, friction dust and the right lead service

A window that sticks is usually described as a carpentry problem. In an older painted assembly, the rubbing surfaces also deserve a lead-safety conversation. Boston-Edison owners may want to keep original features, so the first step is evaluation rather than automatically ordering replacements.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Start with the neighborhood, finish with the property

The Historic Boston-Edison Association describes the district and its residential history. This is useful background for planning work on older architectural features. It is not evidence that a specific sash contains lead or that every house needs the same control. Check the property’s construction and repair records and ask about professional evaluation.

Explain what the window actually does

Does the sash rub against the frame? Is dust collecting in the trough? Does it return after cleaning? Is paint damaged on an accessible sill? Describe those observations and which rooms children use. An inspection can locate lead paint; a risk assessment connects paint condition, dust and other hazards to recommended controls.

Repair, replacement and abatement are not interchangeable

A renovation may repair or replace a window with lead-safe practices. An abatement project is designed to permanently eliminate a documented lead hazard. The proposal should say which project it is and identify the firm’s qualifications. A preservation preference does not decide the hazard-control method; a replacement sales pitch should not decide it either.

Keep exterior approval in the timeline

If your property is subject to local historic-district controls, discuss exterior changes with the Historic District Commission before committing to a new window. Ask what can be retained and what documentation is needed. Resolve that alongside the lead plan so workers do not improvise once the opening is exposed.

What to ask before signing

Request the component list, containment and cleanup arrangements, occupant plan and final check. Ask who examines the work and what happens if samples require corrective work. Keep the reports for future owners and contractors. A painted-over sill can look better without answering whether friction dust or contamination remains.

Common questions

Do original windows have to be replaced if they have lead paint?

Not automatically. Repair with lead-safe practices, enclosure and replacement are different options. The proposal should name the project type and the firm's qualifications.

What is friction dust?

Fine dust created when painted parts rub, like a sash moving in its frame. It can collect in window troughs and on sills without dramatic peeling paint.

Build a usable project record

Keep the inspection or assessment, photos of existing conditions, approved plans, the work scope and final documents together. They help the next contractor understand what remains. Do not label a home “lead-free” on the basis of a neat finish or a limited cleanup report. Ask precisely what the evidence establishes.

A downtown building conversion can change who uses a space and how it is maintained. Lead paint planning belongs in that early discussion, before crews disturb old coatings and before the project assumes that commercial and residential rules are the same.

Request a call

Adaptive reuse changes the questions

The Downtown Detroit Partnership discusses office-space conversion in the district. Converting an office building to housing is a different planning problem from repainting an office suite. Document the present use, proposed use, building age and the surfaces the work will disturb.

Commercial-only is not automatically RRP target housing

The EPA renovation rule focuses on applicable pre-1978 housing and child-occupied facilities. Do not automatically apply that residential framework to every downtown storefront or office. At the same time, a commercial classification is not permission to expose workers or occupants to lead dust. Ask the project’s safety and environmental professionals which worker-protection and waste requirements apply.

Separate the investigations

Paint testing, asbestos surveys, structural inspections and other environmental reviews answer different questions. A lead paint report does not establish that all other hazardous materials are absent. For mixed-use or changing-use projects, the scope should say which spaces and components were evaluated and which were not.

Plan access and occupancy

A multi-floor project may have occupied spaces, shared entrances and work occurring in stages. Describe those conditions to the professional preparing the control plan. Ask how occupants, deliveries and later contractors will be kept out of affected areas. Avoid promises about completion or reopening until the findings, approvals and scope are known.

A business-district request that gets a useful answer

Provide the intended use, unit or floor count, construction history, renovation drawings and any existing reports. State whether you need evaluation, permanent hazard control or renovation safety planning. For housing approvals, verify current Detroit requirements directly with BSEED. A lead contractor cannot guarantee a Certificate of Compliance or decide whether a proposed conversion is permitted.

Do residential lead rules apply to an office conversion?

The EPA renovation rule focuses on applicable pre-1978 housing and child-occupied facilities. A conversion to housing changes that analysis, so document the present and proposed use and ask which framework applies.

What should a conversion lead request include?

The intended use, unit or floor count, construction history, renovation drawings and any existing reports, plus whether you need evaluation, permanent hazard control or renovation safety planning.
